newsitem.title: JORDAN: France extends soft loans to Jordan during Chirac visit.
newsitem.headline: France extends soft loans to Jordan during Chirac visit.

text.p: France has agreed loans to Jordan worth 80 million francs ($15 million) during President Jacques Chirac's visit to Amman, Jordan's state news agency Petra said on Thursday.

It said French Finance and Foreign Trade Minister Yves Galland signed the deal with Jordan's Minister of Trade Ali Abu Al-Ragheb. French diplomats said earlier this week the deal would help finance loans in the fields of water, medical equipment, telecommunications, and meteorological equipment.
The protocol, the latest of a series of annual accords, also included a 15 million franc loan to finance French work in upgrading the kingdom's telephone network, Petra said.
The terms of the loan were "excellent" with a nominal one percent interest, it quoted Ali Abu Al-Ragheb as saying.
Talks also covered Jordan's efforts to get Paris, one of its major creditor nations, to reschedule some of its estimated $700 million debt, part of its total $6 billion foreign arrears.
France agreed in July a debt-swap agreement covering 325 million francs of debt, or just under 10 percent of Jordan's outstanding arrears to France.
Under the agreement, part of the debt will be allocated to offer discounts to French firms investing in Jordan.
The ministers also discussed an investment protection law that would help draw French foreign investment into Jordan and reviewed technical assistance provided by Paris to Jordan.
France recently approved a 9.9 million franc grant to Jordan to automate trading on the Amman stock exchange.
Abu Al-Ragheb was quoted as saying Jordan had also asked for France's help in securing better terms for Jordan's membership application to the World Trade Organisation (WTO).

He also asked for French help in complicated talks between Jordan and the European Union (EU) over a new partnership accord that will allow it to become part of the Euro-Mediterranean free trade area by 2010.
Differences over agricultural exports and intellectual property legislation are putting into question a target date for signing an accord by year end, diplomats say.
"The French side showed responsiveness in discussing all the issues," the minister said.
